newsitem.title: GERMANY: Waigel, opposition signal compromise on tax bill.
newsitem.headline: Waigel, opposition signal compromise on tax bill.

text.p: German Finance Minister Theo Waigel and opposition leader Oskar Lafontaine both called on Friday for a quick deal to clear the passage of the 1997 tax bill -- a key part of the government's austerity plans.

Waigel wants to wrap up a 70 billion mark savings package after key welfare cuts were already passed into law. But the tax bill requires the approval of the Bundesrat upper house of parliament, controlled by Lafontaine's Social Democrats (SPD).

"A rapid agreement on the 1997 tax bill would be the right prelude to next year's tasks," Waigel said. "It would be a signal to markets that Germany accepts the challenges of the future. The problems will be decisively solved."
Lafontaine told the chamber: "Most of the work has already been done -- now it must be possible to find a compromise on the tax bill relatively quickly."

Waigel said he was open to discuss all questions on the bill -- part of his strategy to cut Germany's budget deficit next year to within the Maastricht treaty's limit required to qualify for European Economic and Monetary Union.
The treaty states that participants' budget deficits should be at or close to three percent of gross domestic product in 1997 to qualify for the launch of the Euro currency in 1999.

Waigel met regional leaders recently to hammer out details of the tax bill, which foresees the abolition of tax on wealth and productive assets. Further talks are planned next week, and Waigel called on regional leaders to shoulder more of the savings burden.
Lafontaine repeated earlier SPD demands that Waigel drop plans to delay increases in child benefits and personal tax allowances.

Waigel repeated earlier remarks that higher unemployment benefit costs could mean that more savings would have to be found in the 1997 budget, but that he would await tax estimates in November before taking further steps.
The tax bill is expected to be finally passed into law in November.
